questions.question:
**In the following question, one part of the sentence may have an error. Find out which part of the sentence has an error and click the option corresponding to it. If the sentence is free from error, click the "No error" option.**

Can you imagine (1)/ that she has thirty (2)/ five pair of shoes. (3)/ No Error (4)
questions.solution: A pair refers to a set of two things. So ‘1 pair of shoes’ is a correct expression. However, the ‘thirty five’ indicates that there are more than 1 pair of shoes, you should use the plural form ‘pairs’. Since the error lies in part 3 of the given sentence, option 3 is the correct answer.

questions.question:
**In the following question, one part of the sentence may have an error. Find out which part of the sentence has an error and click the option corresponding to it. If the sentence is free from error, click the "No error" option.**

Mr. Gupta, his wife (1)/ and his younger brother (2)/ was present at the station. (3)/ No Error (4)
questions.solution:
The correct answer is: **3**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• **Plural subjects** are always agreed upon by** plural verbs**.

 
 
• For example: My friends and I **were** going to the park.
 
 
 
• Similarly, in this context, 'Mr Gupta, his wife and his younger brother' are **plural subjects**.
 
• Hence, the **verb** that must agree with them should also be** plural**.
 
• Thus, ‘was’ (singular verb) should be replaced by ‘were’ (plural verb).

Therefore, the correct answer is: *Mr. Gupta, his wife and his younger brother **were** present at the station.*

‘The next year’ can be used to specify the following year when there is a sequence of years. E.G. *Mr. Sharma enjoyed the event so much that he organised another the next year. *Here the next year means the following year.

questions.question:
**In the following question, one part of the sentence may have an error. Find out which part of the sentence has an error and click the option corresponding to it. If the sentence is free from error, click the "No error" option.**

Not only we saw (1)/ the President but also (2)/ the Chief Minister of Delhi. (3)/ No Error (4)
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **'1'.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The phrase "Not only" should be followed by a verb to match the construction with "but also," ensuring parallelism in the sentence.
 
• The correct structure should be "Not only did we see" instead of "Not only we saw" since the verb "did" facilitates the correct formation of an anticipated action when using "not only... but also."
 
• In sentences involving correlative conjunctions like "not only... but also," maintaining the same grammatical structure on both sides is crucial.
 
 
• For example, "Not only did we enjoy the show but also the dinner" showcases proper structure and parallelism.
 
 
 
• Using "did we" ensures the sentence has the correct auxiliary verb before the subject, making it grammatically accurate.
 
• Correcting the error, the sentence should read: "Not only did we see the President but also the Chief Minister of Delhi."

Therefore, the correct answer is** 'Option 1'.**

** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] Additional Information__**

 
• Option 2 ("the President but also") is grammatically correct and part of the proper structure.
 
• Option 3 ("the Chief Minister of Delhi.") correctly follows the "but also" part and maintains parallelism.
 
• Option 4 ("No Error") cannot be correct because the sentence contains an error as outlined in Option 1.

questions.question:
**The sentence(s) given with blanks are to be filled with an appropriate word(s). Four alternatives are suggested for each question. For each question, choose the correct alternative and click the button corresponding to it.**

He gave me an additional _____ of Rs 800 a month by permission of the manager.
questions.solution:
‘Pay’ and ‘salary’ are dues given in exchange of some work. The given sentence does not convey any such meaning.

A ‘perquisite’ is a benefit which one enjoys or is entitled to on account of one's job or position. An ‘allowance’ is a sum granted as a reimbursement for expenses. The usage of ‘additional’ indicates that the concerned person was not *entitled *to the amount, but received it by permission of the manager. Thus, ‘allowance’ is the best fit answer.

• **'Passed over' **means to be ignored or overlooked, especially in favor of someone else for a position, recognition, or promotion. **(उपेक्षित)**

• **Passed by: **This phrase can mean to go past something or someone. **(के पास से गुजरना)**
 
 
• Example: I passed by your house on my way home but didn't have time to stop.
 
 
 
• **Passed out: **This usually means to lose consciousness. **(बेहोश हो जाना)**
 
 
• Example: He was so tired after the marathon that he passed out as soon as he crossed the finish line.

**In the following question, out of the four alternatives, choose the word which best expresses the meaning of the given word and click the button corresponding to it.**

questions.solution:

• **Epitome -** a person or thing that represents the best or most typical example of a quality or class

 
 
• Example: The athlete was the **epitome** of dedication and hard work, inspiring others with his commitment to his sport.
 
 
 
• **Type-** having the qualities, etc. of the group, person or thing mentioned.
 
 
• Example: I know these** types **of people.
 
 
 
• **Extension -** the action or process of extending or being extended; an additional part that is added to something
 
 
• Example: The company requested an **extension **on the deadline, as they needed more time to complete the project.
 
 
 
• **Ruddy -** having a red or reddish color, especially in the face
 
 
• Example: After spending a day at the beach, his face was** ruddy **from the sun.
 
 
 
• **Lively -** full of energy and enthusiasm; active and animated
 
 
• Example: The party was **lively**, with guests dancing and laughing all night long.
 
 
 
• We can identify that the meaning of 'epitome' is closest to that of 'type'.

Therefore, the correct answer is:** type**.

• **Spurious -** false or fake; not genuine or authentic

 
 
• Example: The company was caught selling **spurious** products, which were labeled as luxury items but were actually cheap imitations.
 
 
 
• **Bitter -** having a harsh, unpleasant taste; showing resentment or disappointment
 
 
• Example: The medicine tasted **bitter**, but the patient knew it would help them feel better.
 
 
 
• **Gloomy - **dark or dim; lacking in cheer or hope

• **Fake -** not genuine; counterfeit or artificial
 
 
• Example: The watch that he bought turned out to be **fake**, as it stopped working after just a few days.

• Example: The movie character acted **dumb** and made foolish decisions that led to his downfall.
 
 
 
• As we can see, the meaning of 'spurious' is closest to that of 'fake'.

questions.question:
**Below are three alternatives which may be used to improve the sentence by replacing the words given in the brackets. You may choose option 1, 2 or 3. In case no improvement is needed, choose 4.**

Before I met Sakshi, I (had had) a bad opinion of her.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is: **No improvement**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• In the given sentence, "had had" is used correctly as the** past perfect tense**.
 
• The past perfect tense is used to indicate that an action was completed before another action took place in the past. In this sentence, the action "had had a bad opinion of her" occurred before the action of meeting Sakshi.
 
• Let's break down the sentence to better understand the usage of "had had":
 
 
• Before I **met** Sakshi: This part of the sentence sets the context and establishes the** point in time in the past** when the action took place.
 
• I **had had** a bad opinion of her: This is the **past perfect tense**. The first "had" is the **auxiliary verb** and the second "had" is the **past participle** of the verb "have".
 
 
 
• The use of the **past perfect tense** emphasizes that the opinion was formed **before** the meeting took place. If we had used the simple past tense, the sentence would have been: "Before I met Sakshi, I had a bad opinion of her." This sentence would have conveyed the same meaning, but the past perfect tense emphasizes the sequence of events more clearly.
 
• In summary, "had had" is the past perfect tense and is used to show that an action was completed before another action in the past.

Therefore, the correct answer is: **No improvement**.

**Below are three alternatives which may be used to improve the sentence by replacing the words given in the brackets. You may choose option 1, 2 or 3. In case no improvement is needed, choose 4.**

When I lived in Kanpur I (was going) for movie once a week.
questions.solution: The simple past form ‘lived’ indicates that the action happened in the past and no longer continues. Was going on the other hand depicts that the concerned action was in progress during another action that was taking place in the past. E.G. *I was taking a nap when Sushma rang the door bell. *Thus, ‘used to go’ is the correct replacement of the words given within the brackets.

questions.question:
**Below are three alternatives which may be used to improve the sentence by replacing the words given in the brackets. You may choose option 1, 2 or 3. In case no improvement is needed, choose 4.**

Abhishek was going to the church (then Neha came on to) meet him.
questions.solution: ‘When’ is the conjunction which is used to join an action which takes place during the time another action is taking place. Also, in such sentences, the past continuous tense is used to express the long action (Abhishek was going to the church). And the short action that happens in the middle of the long action (Neha came to meet) is expressed in simple past tense. All these criteria are fulfilled if option 3 is used in place of the words mentioned within the brackets.

questions.question: Why science and religion are considered to be irreconcilable?

options.text: Both relates to the present world
Both arrives to conclusions in which tangible realities are organized
Both differs in their spheres of activity and methods
Modes of actions of both are similar to each other

questions.solution:
The correct answer is **'Both differs in their spheres of activity and methods'**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• The **second **line of the **first **paragraph in the given passage states the following - 

 
 
• *The two, it is commonly declared, are poles apart; their spheres of activity and their methods differ widely, so much so that they are considered to be irreconcilable.*
 
 
 
• Thus we can conclude that because of difference in their spheres of activity and their widely differing methods religion and science are irreconcilable.
 
• Hence, **option 3 **is the correct answer.

questions.question: What can be the suitable title for the passage?

options.text: Science and Religion – Possibility of Reconcile

questions.solution:
The correct answer is **'Science and Religion'**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• The given passage elaborates how science and religion are different as they are based on different methods and activities.
 
• At no point does the passage prove either of the two to be superior or inferior.
 
• The passage also does not present any ground on which the two ideas can be reconciled or go in hand in hand as both them are poles apart.
 
• Thus, **‘Science and Religion’ **is the most suitable title for the passage.
 
• Hence, **option 4 **is the correct answer.
